newsitem.title: UK: CBI - Stg strength squeezed export demand in Feb.
newsitem.headline: CBI - Stg strength squeezed export demand in Feb.

text.p: The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said on Thursday that export demand for UK manufactured goods weakened in February, while overall demand for goods was little changed.
"These results confirm that manufacturers' exports are being squeezed by the upward march of sterling," Sudhir Junankar, associate director of economic analysis at the CBI said in a statement.
But it added that UK firms remained fairly upbeat about stepping up production in the coming months as domestic demand for manufacturing goods continued to hold up.

"The latest CBI monthly trends survey showed 19 percent of firms considered their export order books were above normal, while 31 percent said they were below normal, leaving a negative balance of 12 percent," the CBI said.

"While the overall economic outlook remains healthy, there is a less robust projection for the manufacturing sector as exports and profits growth come under pressure," Kate Barker, the CBI's chief economic advisor, said.
She said low inflation in the manufacturing sector would moderate inflationary prssures from rapid private consumption growth.
"We continue to expect that interest rates should only be increased modestly in 1997, but on present data a rate rise is not yes justified," Barker said.
The CBI survey found a positive balance of four percent of manufacturers expect domestic prices to increase over the next four months.

"Those figures, significantly down on the previous two months, shows the rising trend in price expectations apparent since last October has fallen away, pointing to a promising outlook for output prices."
It added that firms have also scaled back their expectations for securing domestic price rises over the short term.
Stocks of finished goods continue to be more than adequate in relation to expected demand, although less so than in the previous four months.
Output expectations strengthened for the second successive month, following a fall last December. But expectations are still less positive than those recorded between July and November last year.
